The good news

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening3
2 minMake them say the numbers back. Two facts do the emotional work here: every answer is a letter (so this paper has none of the writing risk of Paper 1), and you hear everything twice (so it is fairer than it feels). Confirm from the actual question paper: "There are 40 questions on this paper. Answer all questions." and "You will have 6 minutes to transfer your answers... onto the multiple choice answer sheet." Also note the paper says "Dictionaries are not allowed." So no dictionary — but also remember every answer is a letter, so you rarely need one.
What is being tested

Four skills, from easy to hard

Every question on the paper is testing one of these four. Knowing which one tells you what kind of answer to expect.

L1

Stated facts

Times, places, numbers, names. Said out loud plainly.

“The train leaves at 9:15.”

L2

Opinions

How someone feels about something. Said in opinion words.

“Honestly, it was a waste of money.”

L3

Connections

Linking two ideas — cause, effect, contrast, time.

“Because the buses stopped, she walked.”

L4

Implied meaning

The answer is never said. You work it out.

“Well… I suppose the seats were comfortable.”

Key
24 of the 40 marks involve L4 — Exercises 2, 4 and 5 all test implied meaning. If you only listen for stated facts, you are playing for about 16 marks.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening4
4 minThe intellectual spine of the workshop. Do not read the cards — demonstrate them. Say each example sentence and ask which skill it tests. The number that changes how students listen: L4 (implied meaning) is tested in Exercises 2, 4 and 5 — that is 24 of the 40 marks. A student who hunts only for stated facts caps themselves at roughly 16. Do not claim the answer is never literally present in an L4 question — it IS present, just not in the option words. The option is a paraphrase of the meaning, never a copy of the words. Which is exactly why the next slides matter.

The method

One routine, used on every question of every exercise. Learn it once, use it forty times.

3 minWalk down the Ex column only, then land the three cards. The strategic message: Exercises 1 and 3 are the cheapest 16 marks on the paper (they test L1–L3 only), and Exercise 4 is the heaviest work for the fewest marks (six speakers plus eight statements for 6 marks). The method

T.A.C.O. — four beats, every question

T

Target

Before the audio: read the question and all the options. Underline the key words.

This is where free marks are won.

A

Attend

Hearing 1: get the topic and the shape of the recording. Put a small pencil dash by a possible answer.

Nothing is final yet.

C

Confirm

Hearing 2: listen narrowly. Check your dash, then ask “which option is the trap?”

Change only for a reason.

O

Output

Circle your final letter. Never leave a blank. Move on immediately.

The next extract is about to start.

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening7
4 minMake this physical. Have every student hold up a pen and show you what a "dash" (A) looks like versus a "circle" (C/O). If they cannot tell the two apart on the page they will not know whether they have committed. The single most common failure is skipping T: listening with unread options, hearing one familiar word, and locking it in. That is precisely how the paper is designed to catch them. Stress O: never leave a blank, and do not re-open a question you have committed to — the next extract starts within seconds and needs full attention.
The method

Hearing 1 and hearing 2 are different jobs

Hearing 1Hearing 2
Your jobUnderstand the whole recording — who, what, in what orderDecide each answer with evidence
Your penA small dash by a possible answerA firm circle round the final letter
Your eyesMostly on the question paperMostly listening, glancing at your two best options
NeverLock an answer in — it is only a draftRe-read every option from the beginning
Listen for
not · never · only · already · instead · unless · but · actually · in the end · at first
These words are where the answer flips. Most wrong answers are decided by one of them.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening8
3 minThis is the highest-value behaviour change in the workshop. Most mid-band candidates use hearing 1 to answer and hearing 2 to check they were right — so hearing 2 does no new work. Teach the split: hearing 1 builds the map, hearing 2 plants the flag. Write the flip-words on the board and make them chant once: not, never, only, already, instead, unless, but, actually, in the end, at first. In the real 2025 paper these words decide Question 1 (the park), Question 6 and Question 13 (the café). Also give the inter-hearing ritual: when the recording stops, do not relax — finalise your letter, then glance at the next question. The pause after each extract is 5 seconds, and that is where a disciplined student steals a mark.

Part two

Exercise by exercise

Five exercises. Real questions from the October/November 2025 paper. Each time: you decide first, then we look at the transcript together.

—Section divider. Tell them how it will run: for each exercise they see a real question, get the real reading time, and commit to an answer on paper before you reveal the audio script. Emphasise that committing — even wrongly — is what makes the trap visible.
Exercise 1 · 8 marks

Eight short extracts. One picture question each.

  • 8 separate extracts — 30 seconds each, played twice
  • One question, four pictures A–D
  • Answers are always a concrete thing: a place, a time, an activity
  • No reading pause. You get 3 seconds, then it starts
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening11
3 minBoth images are from the real paper — the instruction box and Question 1. Let them look at Question 1 for a moment; you will use it properly on the next two slides. Say the important structural fact: Exercise 1 has no reading pause. The recording starts with only a three-second gap before Question 1. So for Exercise 1 the "T" step of T.A.C.O. has to be fast and done the moment the paper is in your hands. In practice you should skim all eight Exercise 1 questions before the exam audio begins at all — during the instructions.
Exercise 1 · technique

Four pictures are one question at four settings

Find the difference

Do not read the pictures one by one. Ask:

What single thing changes from A to B to C to D?

That one thing is the question. In Question 1 it is where the car is parked — nothing else matters.

Then predict the words

Once you know the axis, pre-load the vocabulary you expect to hear:

  • Place options → car park, station, petrol station, supermarket, outside, round the corner
  • Time options → o'clock, half past, quarter to, delayed, brought forward
  • Activity options → swimming, cycling, cooking, reading

Now the audio confirms instead of surprising you.

Watch out
When two pictures look almost the same, the answer is one of those two. That is where the exam puts the real decision.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening12
3 minThe core insight: four pictures are not four ideas — they are one idea at four settings. Make them practise naming the axis out loud. Show any Question 1 option set and ask "what single thing changes?" Then teach pre-loading vocabulary. This is the single cheapest technique in the whole paper: if the four options are places, the words car park, station, petrol station, supermarket should be in your head before the audio starts. Recognition beats comprehension under time pressure. The near-duplicate rule is worth stating: when two options are almost identical, the discrimination is between them, because otherwise the option would not exist.

Question 1 — you have 3 seconds

Play Question 1
The real recording, played twice
--:--
The audio says
“there wasn't a single space left in the pool car park… I hope you didn't leave it at the train station like last time… It's actually next to the petrol station… the supermarket's nearer… but I'd feel bad parking there without doing any shopping!”
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening13
4 minRun it properly. Show Question 1, give them ten seconds, and make everyone write a letter before you reveal anything. Then press R. Most classes split between A (petrol station), B (supermarket) and D (train station). That is the perfect teaching moment, because three of the four pictures are mentioned in the audio: D train station — mentioned as a past mistake ("like last time", "I would never make that mistake again"). B supermarket — considered and rejected ("I'd feel bad parking there without doing any shopping"). C pond — never mentioned at all. A petrol station — the only one that is actually true ("It's actually next to the petrol station"). So the answer is A. The rule: the answer is what is true at the END of the extract, not what is said during it.
Real question · Exercise 1

Why A is right — and how the other three are built

Girl: How was swimming club?  Dad: Great, but I'm pretty tired.
Dad: I'm afraid we've got a bit of a walk to the car — there wasn't a single space left in the pool car park.
Girl: I hope you didn't leave it at the train station like last time — that's miles away.
Dad: I would never make that mistake again! It's actually next to the petrol station, which is much better.
Girl: I suppose so, but the supermarket's nearer, and that's got a huge car park.
Dad: Yes, but I'd feel bad parking there without doing any shopping!

A · Petrol station

“It's actually next to the petrol station.” The final, true fact.

B · Supermarket

Suggested by the girl — and refused: “but I'd feel bad…”

C · By the pond

Never mentioned. It exists only to fill the fourth box.

D · Train station

A past mistake: “like last time… never again.”

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening14
4 minNow show the script and walk it line by line. The whole extract is a chain of four places, three of which are traps. This is what Exercise 1 really tests. Name the trap types as you go, because the names recur all workshop: B is the rejected suggestion (“but I'd feel bad…”), C is the never-mentioned option, D is the past mistake (“like last time”), and the answer is signalled by “actually” — one of the flip-words from earlier. Have them underline “actually” in their own copy of the script. Then say the transferable rule out loud and make them write it: in Exercise 1, the answer is true at the end of the extract.
Exercise 1 · the traps

Four traps, and one rule that beats them all

1 · A number that gets cancelled

“It was going to be ten… no, half past nine.” Wait for the sentence to finish.

2 · The past plan

“I used to park there.” / “That's what I said on Friday.” Old information, not the answer.

3 · The mentioned picture

Shown in the audio as a rejected idea or a mistake. Question 1's supermarket and train station.

4 · The near-miss pair

Two options differ by a tiny detail. Both get spoken. Write both numbers down and decide at the end.

The rule
Ask yourself one question on every Exercise 1 item: “Is this still true at the end?” If it was mentioned but then changed, it is a trap.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening15
3 minThese four traps are all the same idea wearing different clothes, and the rule at the bottom is the whole of Exercise 1: is this still true at the end? Have them practise the rule immediately on the questions they can see: in Question 1 the supermarket was mentioned and then refused, so it fails the test. Set the practice task: the other seven Exercise 1 questions in the paper are all built this way. For homework, do Questions 2 to 8 and write beside each wrong picture the reason it was wrong — rejected, past plan, never mentioned, or near-miss. That labelling is worth more than a mark.

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening16
3 minTwo facts to land. First, the value: 10 marks for five extracts — the best marks-per-minute on the paper. Second, the risk: because two questions come from one recording, one moment of inattention costs two marks. The 15-second pause before every pair is the real gift here. Show them the paper: “Now look at Questions 9 and 10” then a 15-second pause. In 15 seconds you can read two questions and three options each — comfortably — if you are not staring at the ceiling.
Exercise 2 · technique

The two questions usually do different jobs

One is usually a fact

How…? Where…? What kind…? How many…?

The answer is stated. Often winnable on hearing 1.

Mark it F on your paper.

One is usually a stance

Why…? How does she feel…? What made him…?

The answer is an opinion, reason or feeling — and the option will be worded differently from the audio.

Mark it S on your paper.

Do this
Write F or S next to each question during the 15-second pause. Then you can see at a glance which one is still unanswered.
Careful
This is a strong habit, not a rule. Sometimes both questions are facts, or both are stances. Use it to aim your attention — never to guess.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening17
3 minBe honest about the strength of this pattern, as the slide itself says: it is a tendency, not a published design rule. Students who treat it as a rule get caught when both questions are factual. What IS reliable is the underlying distinction: some questions are answered by a stated fact, others by a stance. Teaching students to notice which they face is the point, and writing F or S next to each question turns a vague instruction into a visible checklist they can glance at mid-recording. Then demonstrate on Question 9 and 10 (next slide): Question 9 "How did the boy learn…" is a fact; Question 10 "What made the boy choose…" is a reason — a stance.

Real questions · Exercise 2

Questions 9 and 10 — 15 seconds

Play Questions 9 and 10
The real recording, played twice
--:--
Boy: My presentation today's on the environmental videos I make and upload. This is perhaps simpler than you'd imagine. There are literally thousands of websites and film clips on the internet, each of which contains someone guiding you step-by-step. Attending classes on the topic was totally unnecessary, thanks to that.

So why did I choose the environment as a topic? Well, unlike many students, I'd only developed a passion for it relatively recently, but I realised there were a vast number of issues contained within a single subject, which meant each video could be very different from the last. My marks in environment-related schoolwork have improved greatly as a result.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening18
5 minGive them 15 seconds (use a real timer — it is more convincing), then a letter for each question on paper. Then press R to reveal the script. Question 9 = A (he used lots of online resources). The audio says "thousands of websites and film clips... guiding you step-by-step". Trap C — the short course — is explicitly killed: "Attending classes... was totally unnecessary." Mark the word unnecessary. Question 10 = C (it provided many different aspects to focus on). "a vast number of issues contained within a single subject, which meant each video could be very different". The traps here are the star of the slide. A — long-term interest is contradicted ("only developed a passion... relatively recently"). And B is the cleverest trap on the paper so far: the boy does mention that his marks improved — but as a consequence of the choice, not the reason for it, and nobody suggested it. That is a reversed cause-and-effect trap. Ask the class to find the words that kill each option.

Real questions · Exercise 2

Questions 13 and 14 — another pair

Play Questions 13 and 14
The real recording, played twice
--:--
Girl: Have you been to that new café?
Boy: Yeah — I felt totally at home there from the moment I walked in.
Girl: It's like having coffee and cake at your favourite relative's house. But providing more choice of things to eat'd make it even better.
Boy: It would. I'm so pleased it's open in the evening — it's the perfect time to go.
Girl: It'd be great to hang out there before school too — shame it's shut then. Actually, I might ask if they have any jobs available.
Boy: I can imagine you chatting with the customers.
Girl: I meant in the kitchen. I'm hoping to do a catering course after leaving school and it'd be valuable experience for that. And I'd have some extra cash, of course.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening19
6 minAgain: 15 seconds, commit, then reveal. Question 13 = C (welcoming atmosphere) — "totally at home", "like your favourite relative's house". Question 14 = B (it would help her career aims) — "hoping to do a catering course... valuable experience for that". This extract is unusually rich, so use it fully. Three separate traps: A — opening hours are convenient: the audio says the opposite. Evening is fine, but "shame it's shut" before school. That is a polarity flip. B on Question 13 — a wide variety of food: the girl asks for MORE choice, so the variety is a criticism, not a fact. And the best one — C on Question 14, "she would meet lots of people": that idea comes from the boy ("I can imagine you chatting with the customers") and the girl immediately corrects him: "I meant in the kitchen." That is a wrong-speaker trap inside Exercise 2 — exactly the trap that Exercise 5 is built on. Highlight "I meant in the kitchen" and tell them: when one speaker corrects the other, the correction is the answer.
Exercise 2 · the golden rule

The correct option re-words. The traps repeat.

If an option copies the audio…

…be suspicious, not pleased. Recognising your own word feels safe — that feeling is what the trap is made of.

“more choice of things to eat” → option B, “a wide variety of food” but it was a complaint.

If an option re-words the audio…

…it is often the answer. Learn to spot the four moves:

  • Synonym: shocked → surprised
  • Idiom: at home → welcoming
  • Cause/effect flip: marks improved → why he chose it?
  • Polarity flip: “not cheap” → expensive
Keep a list
Every practice paper, write the audio words on the left and the option words on the right. After three papers you will recognise the moves instantly.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening20
3 minTeach the emotional flip and make it explicit: right now, recognising a word makes you feel safe. We want it to make you suspicious. Then immediately give the caveat, because over-correction is a real risk: for pure factual questions the answer can be word-for-word (Question 1's "petrol station" was literal). So this rule is a check, not the decision. The paraphrase journal is the highest-value homework in the whole workshop. Two columns: audio wording, option wording. Ten entries per paper. That is a personal dictionary of the moves Cambridge actually uses.

Exercise 3 · technique

Use the sentence to cross out wrong options

You can often delete an option before you hear a single word. Ask these three questions about the gap.

1

What kind of word is missing?

A noun, a number, a verb? Cross out anything that cannot fit.

“…on the site of an old ___” → a singular noun. “a parking” is impossible.

2

Which way does the sentence point?

Is it describing something good, or something bad?

“The biggest problem was ___” → something negative. A positive option is wrong already.

3

Can the sentence decide it at all?

Sometimes it cannot. If all three options fit, grammar has nothing to say — and that is useful to know.

“about ___ million years ago” → 200, 250 and 400 all fit. Only the audio decides.

What to do when the sentence cannot decide it — Question 19:
The oldest of the shark species living today appeared about ___ million years ago.    A 200   B 250   C 400
All three are numbers, so all three fit. Do not guess — write # in the margin and listen for which number belongs to which fact. The audio says all three; you have to match them.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening22
4 minOne message on this slide and nothing else: the sentence itself can eliminate options. Walk the three questions in order, and give the class about ten seconds after each one to look at their own paper. Be honest about question 3, because it is the part students get wrong. For Question 19 the gap is "about ___ million years ago" — 200, 250 and 400 are all valid numbers and all three are said in the audio. So the sentence cannot decide it. Say that out loud. Students who are taught that this trick always works lose confidence the first time it does not. What the technique IS reliable for: word class (a gap after "an old" cannot be a verb or an uncountable noun) and direction (a sentence about a "problem" wants something negative). Those two genuinely remove options before the audio starts. Land the habit from the box at the bottom: when all three options fit, write # in the margin and match each number to its fact instead of guessing which number you heard.
Exercise 3 · during the audio

In the margin: symbols, not words

Exercise 3 is long. You cannot hold eight questions in your head, so you write the shape of the talk instead.

Before the audio: number your margin 1–8

+   −   ?   X   →   BUT   #

  • + good news    − bad news    ? not sure yet
  • X ruled out    → cause and effect    BUT a contradiction
  • # a number, a date or a price was said
Not this
Writing words or full sentences. Every word you write is a second you are not listening to.
This
One symbol per question, written on hearing 1. On hearing 2 you look at your symbols and go straight back to the questions you marked ? or X.
If you fall behind
Do not catch up on the question you missed. Find the next question number and rejoin there. Chasing one lost mark is how students lose the next two.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening23
3 minThis slide exists because Exercise 3 is where students run out of working memory. Eight questions and one long talk is more than you can hold in your head, so you write a skeleton instead. Make them do it physically. Tell everyone to number their margin 1 to 8 right now, then copy the seven symbols. Physically doing it once beats describing it five times. The two most useful symbols for the exam are # (a number, date or price was said here) and BUT (a contradiction — the speaker is about to overturn something). Between them they cover most of the traps in Exercise 3. The recovery rule at the bottom right is the one that saves marks: if you lose a question, jump forward, never back. An abandoned question is already gone; the next one is still winnable. Say it twice.

Real questions · Exercise 3

Questions 19, 20, 21 — three numbers each

Play the shark talk
Covers Questions 19, 20 and 21
--:--
Jana Holanova: Several types still found swimming in our oceans have done so for almost 200 million years. Their ancestors emerged around 400 million years ago, but most of these disappeared just over 250 million years ago.

So where does the word ‘shark' come from? Before the sixteenth century the term ‘sea dog' described the large fish that sailors often spotted. A Dutch word — shurck — that roughly translates as ‘bad person' is generally accepted as the likely source.

The largest group, the ground sharks, is made up of just under 300 species, so well over half of the 500 or so varieties that live in our seas today. Of this total, around 450 types live fairly close to the shore.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening24
6 minThis is the single best number-training exercise in the paper, because all three questions offer three numbers and the audio says all three. Give 40 seconds (the real reading time), then reveal. Q19 = A (200). The question asks about "the oldest of the shark species living today" — "several types still found swimming have done so for almost 200 million years". The traps are 400 (the ancestors) and 250 (when most disappeared). Three numbers, all real, one answers the question. Q20 = A (bad person). "shurck — which roughly translates as ‘bad person’ — is the likely source. The traps are B (sea dog — the previous word, a temporal reversal) and C (large fish — what ‘sea dog’ described). Q21 = C (500). "around 500 or so varieties that live in our seas today". Trap A is 300 (only the ground sharks group) and B is 450 (only those close to the shore). Then state the general rule: in Exercise 3, every number you hear belongs to something. Your job is to match the number to the question, not to hear a number. Write the candidate numbers in the margin as you hear them.
Exercise 4 · 6 marks

Six speakers. Eight statements. Two are never used.

Play the Exercise 4 instructions
Statements A–H and the real 30-second reading pause
--:--
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening25
4 minRead the instruction box aloud with the class, because it contains the rules: “choose from the list (A–H) which idea each speaker expresses… Use each letter only once. There are two extra letters which you do not need to use.” So: six speakers, eight statements, each letter used once, two left over. That is now confirmed from the paper itself, not a guess. Then read statements A to H together. Notice how similar some are: A and G and E are all about how the speaker felt; B, D and H are all reactions. Several pairs share a topic but point in different directions — that is the design.
Exercise 4 · the system

Six speakers plus eight statements is too much to remember

So do not remember it. Write it down. This takes ten seconds to set up.

Before speaker 1 — write this in the margin:

A ___   B ___   C ___   D ___
E ___   F ___   G ___   H ___
  • When speaker 2 matches statement F, write 2 beside F.
  • Cross out letters as they are used — no letter twice.
  • At the end, count: 6 letters used, 2 left over.
  • If two speakers point at the same letter, you know where the mistake is.
Why
The count is a free error detector. Most Exercise 4 mistakes are not mishearings — they are a statement used twice without noticing.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening26
3 minMake them physically build the ledger now, in the margin of their own paper. Physically doing it once beats describing it five times. The core insight: Exercise 4 is a working-memory problem, not an English problem. Six speakers plus eight statements is fourteen items — more than anyone holds reliably. The written ledger is what makes it survivable. The counting trick at the end is the part students never think of: six speakers must consume six different letters, with two left over. If two speakers point at F, there is an error and they know exactly where to look. Also: never leave a speaker blank. A blank scores zero for certain; a reasoned elimination often scores.
Press R to reveal
Real questions · Exercise 4

Speakers 1 and 2 — which statement fits?

Statements A–H are on the previous slide. You have 30 seconds.

Play Speakers 1 and 2
The real recording, played twice
--:--
Speaker 1 (girl, Australian): I took part in a talent show last week, thinking it'd be the first and last time, but my performance showed enough promise to have another go. I'm astonished it went as well as it did, because the first competitor sang the same song as I was due to perform, so I rapidly decided to switch my choice of music. This actually helped reduce my anxiety.

Speaker 2 (boy, UK): I play guitar and decided to enter a talent show at school. Considering I spent every spare minute I had practising the piece of music I chose for it, I would've been amazed if I'd finished last. Even so, I wasn't expecting to be good enough to win, which is what happened. The people watching were mainly parents and family, so it's hardly surprising they clapped everyone so enthusiastically, but it was nice to hear.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening27
6 minGive the real 30 seconds, then commit. Q27 = E (I changed my mind about what I'd perform at the last minute) — "I rapidly decided to switch my choice of music". Q28 = C (I prepared for it as well as I could) — "I spent every spare minute I had practising". Now do the real work: show how many statements are built from the speaker's own words and then reversed. For Speaker 1: A ("I don't think I'll ever enter another one") is undone by "showed enough promise to have another go". And G ("I had never felt so nervous") is undone because the extract says her anxiety was reduced. For Speaker 2: D ("I was sure I was going to come in last place") is the exact reversal — he says he would have been amazed to finish last. And H ("I was amazed by the audience's reaction") is undone by "it's hardly surprising they clapped everyone". So three of the eight statements are traps made of the speakers' own vocabulary, flipped. Ask the class to name the flip-words: but, hardly, reduced, never again.
Exercise 5 · 8 marks

One interview. Eight questions. One speaker who counts.

Play the Exercise 5 instructions
Hear the real 45-second reading pause
--:--
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening28
4 minRead the instruction line with them: "You will hear an interview with a competitive skateboarder called Mikaela Quayle." Then the key sentence from the syllabus — the questions test information expressed by the main speaker. Define "main speaker" operationally: the person being interviewed, the one who answers. The interviewer is scaffolding. That gives the most important habit in Exercise 5: before you hear a word, decide which voice is the one that counts and mark it on your paper. Then as you listen, tag every opinion as INT or MAIN. Also flag the 45 seconds: this is the longest reading pause in the paper, and it is there because there are eight questions.
Exercise 5 · technique

Ask “who said it?” before “is it true?”

The interviewer is a trap factory

The interviewer asks, guesses and summarises. Any of those can be turned into a wrong option — because they are in the audio.

“So it was all about the charity, then?”
“You must have been exhausted?”

Those are questions, not facts. The answer is in the main speaker's reply — especially if they correct it.

Wait for the correction

When the main speaker disagrees with the interviewer, the correction is the answer. Listen for:

not exactly · well, not quite · that's not how I'd put it · I meant…

And distrust the interviewer's summary: the rebuttal that follows it is where the mark is.

The habit
Tag every opinion in your head: INT says… or MAIN says…. It costs nothing and it removes the single most common Exercise 5 error.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening29
3 minAttribution is the Exercise 5 skill. Name it and make it a habit: mentally prefix every opinion with INT or MAIN. Two versions to teach. First, the interviewer's guess becomes a wrong option ("You must have been exhausted?") — students mark it because it sounds like a description of the situation, but it is a question. Second, the interviewer's summary becomes a wrong option, and the main speaker rebuts it. Give them the correction markers: not exactly, well not quite, that's not how I'd put it, I meant. And point back: this exact trap already appeared in Exercise 2, when the girl corrected the boy — "I meant in the kitchen." It is one idea appearing across exercises.
Press R to reveal
Real questions · Exercise 5

Questions 33 and 34 — the interview begins

Play Questions 33 and 34
The interview begins here
--:--
Interviewer: I'm talking to fifteen-year-old Mikaela Quayle. How did it start?
Mikaela: I was learning to walk and Dad noticed I hardly ever fell over. As a skateboarder himself, he said, ‘Let's put her on a skateboard' — I was eighteen months old! I couldn't do anything, but the balance was there. I've no memory of that, but I was never without my skateboard as I grew up. Other kids take toys on car journeys — I had my skateboard!

Mikaela: When I was three, Dad took me to the skateboard park. I just stayed at the bottom. I didn't necessarily admire the older skaters, I just felt I was one of them. I wanted to try tricks, and was shocked when I realised how hard it was. But I didn't give up and eventually managed a small jump.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening30
6 min45 seconds of reading time, then commit. Q33 = C (she has forgotten first getting on a skateboard) — "I've no memory of that". Q34 = B (surprised by the challenges involved) — "I was shocked when I realised how hard it was"; shocked re-worded as surprised. The traps are worth more than the answers here. Q33 option A — "she refused to use any transport other than her skateboard". The audio says she was "never without" it and took it on car journeys. That is close, but "refused any other transport" is an overstatement — a degree shift. Q33 option B — "she hoped to satisfy her father's dreams". The audio says it was Dad's idea, but nothing about her hoping to satisfy his dreams. That is an invented motive built from real content. Q34 option C — "excited to watch other skateboarders" is directly negated: "I didn't necessarily admire the older skaters." Finish by pointing at the word "shocked": that single word is the whole of Q34, and it is a paraphrase question, not a fact.
Exercise 5 · language

The words that give away an opinion

L2 and L4 questions are won or lost on these phrases. Each column below does a different job.

Column 1

An opinion is coming

to be honest · if I’m honest · I’d say · I suppose · frankly · I must admit

What to do: get ready. The answer is in the next few words.

Column 2

The meaning is about to flip

but · however · although · actually · that said · hardly · only

What to do: cross out whatever came before it. That part is the trap.

Column 3

A feeling, with no feeling word

it grew on me · I could take it or leave it · it left me cold · I wasn’t blown away · it fell flat · not really my thing

Why it matters: the options paraphrase these, so you have to know what each one means.

Build one page
Add every new phrase you meet to a single page in your notes. That page is worth more than another whole practice paper.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening31
4 minThis is a signal slide, not a vocabulary list. The three columns do three different jobs, so teach them as three separate instructions rather than as one list of words. Column 1 tells you an opinion is arriving. Demonstrate it live: say "if I'm honest, …" and have the class say "here it comes" back to you. When a speaker uses any of those phrases, the answer is in the next clause. That is the whole of column 1. Column 2 is the highest-value family in the entire paper. Everything before but / however / actually / that said is the decoy. You can prove it from questions they have already seen: Question 1 ("it's actually next to the petrol station"), Question 13 ("shame it's shut"), Question 10 ("improved greatly as a result" — a consequence, not a reason) and Speaker 1 in Exercise 4. Make that connection out loud: it is one idea reappearing in every single exercise. Column 3 is a vocabulary job, and it is finite. "It left me cold", "it fell flat", "I could take it or leave it" are exactly the kind of hedged evaluation that options paraphrase into "she was disappointed". If a student does not know the phrase, the mark is gone before technique can help. Set the task at the bottom: one page, added to after every practice paper. Not a textbook list — their own list.
03
Part three

Using the transcript

The transcript is the answer key for everything you just practised. Used properly, it is the fastest way to raise your score — and almost nobody uses it.

1 minSet up the section. Most students finish a past paper, check their score, and put it away. That wastes the paper. The transcript shows you exactly which words decided each answer — and it is the only way to find out whether a mistake was a mishearing or a wrong decision. Tell them plainly: a paper you do not review teaches you almost nothing, because you simply rehearse your existing habits.
Review

A paper without a review is a wasted paper

What most students do

  • Do the paper, count the score, close the file.
  • Say “I misheard it” and move on.
  • Repeat the same mistakes in the next paper.
  • Never find out which word decided the answer.

What raises your score

  • Do the paper, then open the transcript.
  • Find the exact phrase that earns each mark.
  • Name the trap that caught you.
  • Add the wording to your paraphrase list.
Rule
A blank scores zero, but a mistake you have diagnosed is worth marks next time. One reviewed paper beats three unreviewed ones.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening33
3 minThe key line is at the bottom: one reviewed paper beats three unreviewed ones. Students default to volume; we want diagnosis. Ban the phrase "I misheard it". It is not diagnostic and it leads to no change. Instead they must name the reason: cancelled number / past plan / rejected suggestion / wrong speaker / polarity flip / degree shift / never mentioned. Show them the arithmetic of why this matters: if they are losing, say, six marks a paper and diagnose only two of them, the other four will repeat all year. Diagnosing five of six is a different trajectory entirely.
How to read a transcript

Four things to look for on every page

R1  Question 1
Where did the girl's dad park their car?
PAUSE 00'03"
M: male, forties, UK accent
F: female, mid-teens, UK accent
M: How was swimming club?
F: Great, but I'm pretty tired.
M: …I'm afraid we've got a bit of a walk to the car…
[ end of extract ]
PAUSE 00'05"
REPEAT FROM * TO **
1

M: and F:

Each speech bubble is labelled, so you can check who said it — not just what was said.

2

Voice descriptions

“male, forties, UK accent” tells you which voice is which before you replay.

3

Every PAUSE

The 5-second gap after each extract is where you commit your letter.

4

REPEAT FROM * TO **

Shows exactly which part is played twice, so you can replay only that.

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening34
4 minHand out the transcript (pages 2 onward) and look at the real thing together. Walk the four features on the left-hand sample. The most useful one for teaching is number 1: the speaker labels. Because the transcript marks M and F line by line, you can prove to a student that their wrong answer came from the other speaker — which is the whole of the Exercise 5 technique, made visible. This is also how you demonstrate the café extract (Question 14): the boy says "chatting with the customers", the girl says "I meant in the kitchen". Point out that the transcript also records the PAUSE times, which is how we know your reading time is 15 seconds in Exercise 2 and 45 seconds in Exercise 5. Practical tip: the transcript is a teacher document, so keep the paper itself clean. Give students the transcript after they have attempted the questions, never before.
The 4-step drill

How to review a paper in twenty minutes

Step 1

Do it properly first

Full speed, one play, no pausing. Write a letter for all 40 — including guesses.

Step 2

Mark it, but do not look at the answers

Just look at which questions were wrong. Do not read the transcript yet.

Step 3

Now open the transcript

For each wrong question, find and underline the phrase that earns the mark. Then write why you were wrong: which trap?

Step 4

Replay only those extracts

Listen again with the script in front of you. Your ear connects the written phrase to the sound.

Write this
Beside every wrong answer, write one of: rejected suggestion · past plan · never mentioned · wrong speaker · polarity flip · degree shift · number for something else
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening35
3 minThis is the method you want them to actually use at home, so keep it concrete and time-boxed. Step 3 is the one that must not be skipped — underline the phrase, name the trap. Step 2 matters more than it looks: mark it without reading the answers first, otherwise reviewing becomes reading rather than diagnosing. Step 4 is where the real learning happens for weaker listeners: hearing the phrase while looking at it written is what connects the sound to the words. This is the same idea as the micro-listening drill, and it is why the transcript is so valuable. Set this as the standing homework for every practice paper from now on, and give the list of trap names at the bottom as the vocabulary they must use.
04
Part four

Exam craft

The six minutes that decide your paper, the mistakes that cost the most, and a four-week plan you can start tomorrow.

1 minLast section. Signal the shift: everything so far was about listening; this part is about the mechanics of the exam room, where marks are lost for reasons that have nothing to do with English.
Exam craft · the last 6 minutes

Forty letters. Six minutes. Do not lose them here.

5:00
transfer time
1:00
final check
  • Transfer in blocks of five. Check each block. Then move on.
  • Cover the lines below with your hand — this is the single best fix for line errors.
  • Shade one letter per question. Erase completely if you change your mind.
  • Sweep at the end: no blanks, no double-shaded lines, and your last answer is on line 40.

The three silent disasters

Off by one. Everything right, everything on the wrong line.

Double-shaded. Two letters on one line.

Blank line. A blank is worth zero for certain.

Check
Count the answer lines as you finish. If your final answer is on line 40, your transfer is almost certainly aligned.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening37
4 minDo this one physically if you can — hand out a real multiple-choice answer sheet and have them shade five blocks while covering the lines below with their hand. It takes three minutes and it removes an entire category of loss. The numbers are real: the transcript shows a five-minute pause and then a further one-minute pause before the end of the examination — the six minutes for transferring. That is about nine seconds per line, which is comfortable. The risk is not time, it is mechanical error. Emphasise the count check, because it is arithmetic they already trust: 8 + 10 + 8 + 6 + 8 = 40. If the last answer lands on line 40, the transfer is aligned. If it lands on 39, a line was skipped and there is still time to find it. And say the unpopular thing: a blank line is a certain zero. Never leave one.
Exam craft

Eight mistakes that cost marks every year

1 · Not reading the options

Listening to an unread question is the single biggest cause of wrong answers.

2 · Choosing the option you recognise

A familiar word is bait, not proof.

3 · Missing the “but”

Everything before the pivot is the decoy.

4 · Answering from the interviewer

Right idea, wrong speaker. Ask who said it first.

5 · Re-reading everything on hearing 2

You do not have time. Narrow to your two candidates.

6 · Chasing a lost question

Jump to the next number. One lost mark becomes three this way.

7 · Writing words in the margin

Numbers and symbols only. Every word is a second not listening.

8 · Leaving a blank

A guess sometimes scores. A blank never does.

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening38
3 minDo not read all eight aloud — that is a wall of text and they will switch off. Ask instead: "put your hand up if number 3 sounds like you… number 1?… number 8?" You will find the same three or four attract almost everybody, and that is the point: the losses are clustered and predictable. Then set the ritual that fixes them: each student writes their own two worst mistakes on the front of every practice paper before starting, and ticks them off at the end. Trivial to do, and it works. If you only fix one, fix number 1. Reading the options in the silence is free and it is worth several marks.
From today

A four-week plan

Week 1

Find your pattern

  • One paper, then review with the transcript
  • Name the trap for every wrong answer
  • Start your paraphrase page

Output: your two weakest traps.

Week 2

Fix Exercise 1 and 3

  • Questions 1–8 and 19–26 of two more papers
  • Label every wrong picture: rejected / past / never said
  • 5 min of transcript listening, 3× this week

Output: Exercise 1 at 7 or 8 out of 8.

Week 3

Attack 2, 4 and 5

  • One full paper under exam conditions
  • Re-do only Exercises 2, 4, 5 with the transcript
  • Quote the phrase that earns each mark

Output: every answer traced to a phrase.

Week 4

Rehearse it

  • Two papers, timed, with the real answer sheet
  • Practise the 6-minute transfer with a pen
  • No new words this week — technique only

Output: a routine you do not have to think about.

Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening39
3 minPresent it as four focuses rather than four calendar weeks — adapt to your timetable. The discipline that makes it work is the one rule from the transcript section: never do a paper without reviewing it. Week 2 targets the cheap marks: Exercises 1 and 3 test L1 to L3 only and are 16 marks between them. The measurable milestone is Exercise 1 at 7–8 out of 8. Week 3 targets the 24 mark block — Exercises 2, 4 and 5 — and its discipline is the licensing quote: no quote, no mark. Week 4 is rehearsal only, including the mechanical transfer on a real answer sheet. Tell them explicitly: no new vocabulary in the last week. It is for stabilising a routine, not adding material.
Be honest with yourself

Six things to be able to say yes to

Tick only the ones that are true under exam conditions — not the ones that are true when you are relaxed.

1. I read all the options during the silence, every time.

2. I write a dash on hearing 1 and circle on hearing 2 — never the same job twice.

3. I can name what caught me: rejected, past plan, wrong speaker, polarity flip.

4. In Exercise 4 I build the A–H ledger before speaker 1.

5. In Exercise 5 I ask who said it? before is it true?

6. I never leave a blank, and I have never been off by one on the answer sheet.

Scoring
5–6 yes: your technique is ready — keep the practice loop going.  3–4 yes: pick your two weakest and make them your focus for three weeks.  0–2 yes: do not do more papers — fix the routine first.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening40
3 minHave them tick honestly in pencil and count. The point of the scoring bands is to normalise the middle: most strong candidates land at 3 or 4, and that is a target list, not a failure. Each statement maps to a slide in this deck, so a student can self-serve the remedy: statement 1 → the T.A.C.O. slide; 2 → two hearings; 3 → the trap slides; 4 → the Exercise 4 ledger; 5 → the Exercise 5 attribution habit; 6 → the transfer slide. Tell them this — it turns the checklist into a revision map. The 0–2 band matters most and is the one to say out loud: if that is you, more papers will not help. The routine has to change first.
Take these with you

Six things to remember

Read before you listen

The paper gives you 15, 30, 40 and 45 seconds. Use all of it.

Two hearings, two jobs

Hearing 1 maps it. Hearing 2 decides it.

Distrust the words you recognise

The answer usually re-words. The trap usually repeats.

Hunt the pivot

but · however · actually · not · instead · hardly. The answer comes after.

Ask who said it

Especially in Exercise 5. The interviewer is a trap factory.

Review with the transcript

One diagnosed paper beats three papers you never checked.

Remember
Paper 2 is not mainly a test of how much English you know. It is a test of how well you handle a recording you only hear twice. That is a skill — and skills improve with practice.
Falih Junior International Academy  ·  IGCSE English as a Second Language 0511  ·  Paper 2 Listening41
3 minDo not re-teach this — use it as a retrieval quiz instead. Cover the slide, read out the six headings one at a time, and ask the class to recall the detail before you reveal it. Retrieval practice beats re-reading, and it takes the same three minutes. The closing framing is the message of the whole workshop and it is genuinely liberating for a strong class: you already have the English. What separates a 26 from a 34 at this level is not more vocabulary — it is the routine. If you want a single sentence for them to leave with: read before you listen, decide on the second hearing, distrust the words you recognise, and never leave a blank.

Good luck.

This week

Label every wrong answer in one paper with the trap that caught you.

Every week

One paper, always reviewed with the transcript.

Until the exam

Five minutes of transcript listening, three times a week.
